text: Sometimes the data you need lives on a web page, with no API and no download button anywhere. Web scraping means fetching a page's HTML with code and extracting the parts you need. It's a useful last resort, but unlike an API, it's not something the site has promised to support, so it comes with real technical fragility and real ethical responsibilities. We start with the responsibilities, then build a small working scraper.

Before you scrape anything, ask four questions. Is there an API or a downloadable file? If yes, use that instead — it's more stable and clearly permitted. What does robots dot txt say? Most sites publish one describing which paths automated tools should avoid — it's a widely followed convention, not a law, but ignoring it is poor practice regardless. What do the terms of use say? Many sites prohibit scraping outright, whatever robots dot txt says, and some data carries copyright or privacy concerns on top of that — when in doubt, ask the site owner, or don't scrape. And scrape gently — a descriptive user agent, requesting only what you need, pausing between requests, and stopping if asked.

We'll practice on Books to Scrape, a fictional bookstore built specifically as a sandbox for learning this — never assume a real commercial site is fair game the same way. Python's standard library includes a robots dot txt parser — point it at the site's robots file, read it, and ask can underscore fetch whether you're allowed in. This particular site returned a 404 for robots dot txt, meaning no rules are published, so can underscore fetch returns True. Then fetch the page, identifying yourself clearly with a descriptive User-Agent header.

Resp dot text is just a long string of HTML. Beautiful Soup turns it into a tree you can search with CSS selectors. Select every article with the class product underscore pod, and you get 20 matching book cards on this page. From the first card, pull the title attribute off its h3 link, and get the visible price text with select underscore one and get underscore text. Select returns every match; select underscore one returns just the first. Right-click any element in your browser and choose Inspect to find the right selector for it.

Loop over every card, building a dictionary of title and price for each one, and collect them into a list. Wrap that list in pd dot DataFrame, and you get a clean table — one row per book, straight from the scraped HTML. Every column comes back as plain text at this point, exactly the kind of thing the cleaning skills from Chapter 5 are built to handle next.

Clean the price column by stripping everything that isn't a digit or a decimal point with a regex replace, then converting with pd dot to underscore numeric — now it's a real float you can average. To cover several pages, loop over page URLs, calling raise underscore for underscore status on each response, and pause one second between requests with time dot sleep to stay gentle. On this site, pages 1 through 3 together gave 60 books total.

If a page happens to contain a plain HTML table, pd dot read underscore html can parse it directly into a list of DataFrames, no manual card-by-card scraping needed — it does need a parser like lxml installed to work.

Scrapers break for three common reasons. Layout changes — the site redesigns, and your selectors silently stop matching, with nothing warning you unless you actually validate the result, the way Lesson 26 taught. JavaScript-generated content — requests only ever sees the initial HTML, never what scripts add to the page afterward. And blocks or rate limits — if a site starts slowing you down or blocking you outright, back off, or stop entirely.

To recap: prefer an API when one exists; check robots dot txt and the terms of use; scrape gently. Requests fetches the HTML, and BeautifulSoup's select extracts the elements you need. Build a list of dictionaries, then a DataFrame, then clean the types the same way you always do. Expect scrapers to be fragile, and validate what they return. Next chapter: writing reliable data code, starting with clean code for notebooks.
